title: Wimbledon Boss Jokes Military Guards Would ‘Sort Out’ Disruptive Influencers
summary:
Wimbledon's chief executive joked that Royal Marine commandos who help secure the famous tennis tournament would love to "sort out" social media influencers who disrupt matches—while still saying influencers matter for modern marketing.

The comments follow a debate that began at the U.S. Open, where organizers accredited about 100 influencers and content creators. A photo shoot during a Naomi Osaka match interrupted play and sparked talk about tennis etiquette. World No. 4 Coco Gauff said welcoming new fans is important but people should "follow the etiquette of the sport."

Speaking on a panel at Leaders Week London, Wimbledon boss Atkinson said the club does not have an official "influencer" accreditation category. Brand partners such as Polo Ralph Lauren may bring creators, he said, but they would be "tightly chaperoned." He praised SW19's tradition of fans quietly respecting the action—what he called a "self-policing" crowd.

Atkinson contrasted the U.S. Open's lively New York atmosphere, where someone with a ticket might start broadcasting mid-match with ring lights, with Wimbledon's stricter mood. Fans will not be allowed to bring portable ring lights to the All England Club. Still, he called a total ban on influencers "nonsense" because marketing now goes far beyond newspapers and TV.

"You've got to sort it out in a Wimbledon way," he said, keeping the tournament's brand and "magic" while adapting to new media. The joke about military security underscored how seriously Wimbledon wants calm courts—even as it courts online creators carefully.
why_it_matters: Sports events are adapting to social media while protecting fair play. Kids can discuss how online fame and real-world manners should share the same space.
